catalog_quote: Logoori is a tone language, and distinguishes two surface tones, H and L (the former marked with acute accent). Lexical strict minimal pairs are rare. [...] However, tonal minimal pairs reflecting grammatical differences are frequent in the language. [...] Viewing tone from the syllabic perspective, there are three surface distinctions, High (H), Low (L) and Fall (F) – additionally, there is a general pitch-register lowering process of downstep (notated with ꜝ) which occurs between H tones. [...] Falling tone only occurs on a long syllable, and is notated as H (accent) on the first vowel, e.g. kodéeka ‘to cook’. F is highly restricted. There are grammatical and lexical contrasts between F and H in the penultimate syllable
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Logooli (logo1258) is not in the catalog. The five works with stress in the title are one comparative thesis (Philippson 1991, Paris 5: ~30 East African Bantu languages on a tonal-to-penultimate-stress continuum; full text not online, theses.fr 'accessible: non', abstract read; Logooli membership in the sample unverified; medium priority for print acquisition) and four bibliographic variants of one paper, Goldsmith 'Tone and Accent in Llogoori' (AAP 25, 1991 = Joy of Grammar 1992, DOI 10.1075/z.55.07gol paywalled), read in full from the author's open scan at people.cs.uchicago.edu. Goldsmith describes Logooli as a tone language (H/L/toneless, downstep, syllable TBU, contrastive length) and posits an abstract quantity-sensitive metrical foot (first syllable extrametrical, iambic foot at left edge of stem) that governs where grammatical High tones dock in the Present Continuous and Middle Future; he states explicitly that there is no phonetic evidence of stress or rhythm. So the item is prosody-but-not-word-stress, not a stress-placement source. Additional open Logooli phonology read as controls: Odden 2019 (Loquens, geminate blockage), Odden 2021 (JUL, substance-free segmental phonology: 'Tone and vowel length do not figure into the present analysis'), Pak 2019 (Florida Linguistics Papers, grammatical tone, adopts Goldsmith's grid) — none mentions word stress or penultimate lengthening. Not obtainable online: Leung 1986/1991 Cornell 'The tonal phonology of Llogoori' (print only; Goldsmith's data source), Odden 2018 'Tonal melodies in the Logoori verb' (Chicago, paywalled), Appleby 1943 Luragoli grammar, Gudahi 2003 (Hathi search-only). No first-hand word-stress statement for Logooli was found; no new stress statement was found.org, theses.fr and direct site downloads.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Logoori is a two-tone language (H vs L, with downstep and a falling tone confined to long penultimate syllables) with contrastive vowel length; the most authoritative description (Odden's online reference grammar) and every other opened description are silent on word stress, and Goldsmith 1991 states explicitly that his metrical 'accent' has no phonetic stress or rhythm correlate. No source states where word stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Odden ch. 2 p. 22 notes that long vowels far from the right edge may be phonetically shortened in connected speech, 'the historical precursor to loss of vowel length distinctions before the antepenultimate syllables, as exists in Chimiini, Matumbi and Mwera', i.e. an incipient right-edge prominence of length, not phonologized.
new_statements.domain_note: Word and phrase level: Odden's prosody section describes contrastive vowel length and a two-tone (H/L) system with surface Fall restricted to long penults and downstep; tense distinctions are 'only prosodically realized' by tone (ch. 1, p. 3). No word-stress statement anywhere in the grammar, in Leung 1991, or in any other opened source. The only explicit remark on phonetic stress is Goldsmith 1991 (author's scan p. 24, note 9), who places Llogoori among 'cases in which there is no phonetic evidence of alternating stress or overt rhythm' while positing an abstract quantity-sensitive metrical foot at the left edge of the verb stem to place grammatical H tones in the Present Continuous and Middle Future.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Logooli proper (glottocode logo1258; ISO rag), the Luyia variety of Vihiga County, Kenya, under the names Logoori (Odden, Pak), Llogoori (Leung, Goldsmith), Lulogooli (Kenyan theses), Maragoli (Yukawa). Odden's grammar draws on speakers from both North Maragoli (east of Mudete) and South Maragoli (west of Majengo) and notes dialect differences in segments and verb inflection, none concerning stress; Leung's data come from one speaker (Miss Kilibwa), Yukawa's from one Vihiga speaker.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing statement (Odden 2026 grammar: tone language with H/L, no stress statement); adds that Logoori's verb tone system is of the 'conservative' Luyia type with a lexical /H/ vs toneless root contrast and leftward H spreading. new_statements.rule_in_words: Logoori is treated as a 'conservative' Luyia tone language: verb roots contrast /H/ vs toneless, H verbs carry H on the first stem syllable, tense-determined melodic H tones are added in most TAM forms, and H spreads leftward through toneless moras. The article describes Idakho, Nyala-West and Wanga in detail; Logoori is mentioned only in passing. The words stress, accent and prominence do not occur anywhere in the text (0 hits), so nothing is said about word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none about Logoori; the paper's own data are Idakho, Nyala-West and Wanga (p. 124)
new_statements.identity_note: Ebarb, Green & Marlo 2014 place Logoori (JE41) in Maho's Logoori-Kuria group with Idakho, Isukha and Tiriki (p. 122 n. 1) and cite Leung 1991 as the Logoori source; their own detailed data are for Idakho [ida], Nyala-West [nle] and Wanga [lwg], not Logoori. Philippson's thesis is a comparative survey of about thirty East African Bantu languages (abstract); whether Logoori is among them is unknown.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (Odden 2026 grammar) codes Logoori as tonal with H/L(/Fall) and downstep between H tones, no stress statement; Philippson 1991 independently lists Logooli among the languages with downstep and a H-tone/LH-melody prosodic system and says nothing about stress: same type. It also matches the Ebarb, Green & Marlo 2014 statement held by the project (lexical /H/ vs toneless verbs). Adds nothing on stress placement; its Logooli data are second-hand (Leung 1985) and explicitly called deficient.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Philippson treats Logooli (E41, Luhya group VII) as a tone language of the Bukusu-Masaaba type: lexical H tones with a LH (BH) melody, downstep between H tones attested (in certain verb forms), 'posterior' H tones and regressive H dissimilation in the verb system; he says his information on Logooli is too poor for a full analysis (only Leung 1985 on verbs) and gives no statement about word stress or a fixed accent position for Logooli. The thesis's tone-to-penultimate-accent continuum places the Lacustrine/Luhya languages at the tonal end; the demarcative penultimate accent it discusses (ch.6 sec.3.5) concerns Swahili and other coastal/southern languages, not Logooli.

new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's 'logooli (E 41)' = Guthrie E41 Logooli/Maragoli, the Luyia (Luhya, his group VII) language of western Kenya = Glottolog logo1258; his data are second-hand from Leung 1985 (Llogoori verbs, the same Cornell work whose 1986/1991 version is already read held by the project). No dialect distinction is made.

tone_statements.citation: Goldsmith, John A. (1992). Tone and Accent in Llogoori. In Brentari, Larson & MacLeod (eds.), The Joy of Grammar. A festschrift in honor of James D. McCawley, 73-94. Amsterdam: Benjamins.
tone_statements.quote: Llogoori has a tonal system with underlying High (H) and Low (L) tones, but morphemes may be underlyingly toneless as well. As a first approximation, we may say, following Leung (p. 12), that the syllable is the tone-bearing unit of the language ... On the surface, Llogoori has familiar properties of tone languages, including long sequences of syllables pronounced on the same tone (here, pitch level), which may be either Low or High, with a downstepped High as a third possibility. In addition, falling tones are created, though late in the phonology.
tone_statements.locator: p. 2, section 2.1 'Some initial facts about the tone system'
tone_statements.summary: Underlying H vs L (morphemes may be toneless); downstepped H and falling tones are derived. The 'accent' is an abstract quantity-sensitive metrical grid placing grammatical H, not phonetic stress.

sources.quote: The particular conclusion we draw is that Llogoori has developed a quantity-sensitive accentual system quite similar to the familiar quantity-sensitive pattern found in Latin or in English, a pattern in which vowel length determines syllable weight. [...] the present analysis adds to a growing body of literature that supports the position that metrical structure plays a role in the organization of language in a large number of cases in which there is no phonetic evidence of alternating stress or overt rhythm.
sources.note: Llogoori is described as a tone language (H/L, toneless morphemes, downstep, syllable as TBU; p. 2). The 'accent' of the title is an abstract metrical grid (a single quantity-sensitive iambic foot at the left edge of the verb stem, first syllable extrametrical in the Middle Future) that determines where a tense-specific High tone docks in two tenses (Present Continuous, Middle Future); Goldsmith states explicitly that there is no phonetic evidence of stress or rhythm. sources.note: Reanalyses Leung's verb-tone data with an abstract quantity-sensitive metrical grid (first syllable extrametrical, iambic foot) that places grammatical H tones in two tenses. States that such metrical prominence 'does not surface as any particular phonetic effect' (Chimwiini comparison, p. 20) and that the analysis belongs to 'cases in which there is no phonetic evidence of alternating stress or overt rhythm' (note 9, p. 24). No word-stress location given.

sources.quote: For the practicing accentologist [...] the pattern is a clear one: it is the Latin stress rule, viewed through a mirror. Scanning rightward from the beginning, rather than leftward from the end as in Latin, we skip the first syllable, and then assign an accent to the next syllable (the second) if it is heavy, and skip it if it is light, assigning accent to the following syllable [...] Metrical theory informs us that the proper statement is: (1) assign extrametrical status to the first syllable; (2) assign a Q-sensitive iambic foot to the left end of the stem
sources.note: Original AAP version of the same paper (Pak 2019 cites it as AAP 25: 7-30). The 'accent' is a grid used to place grammatical High tones in two verb tenses, built on Leung's (1986/1991) Llogoori verb-tone data; it is tone assignment, not phonetic stress. No statement of word-stress location.
